A ghost keeps changing shells.

A new Ghost in the Shell animation entered production yesterday. The 1989 manga’s most durable prediction may be the franchise’s own ability to migrate from one creative body to another.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 24, 2026 at 09:20 JST · 7 min read

Before smartphones, social networks or consumer artificial intelligence, Shirow Masamune drew a world in which identity could move through networks and bodies could become platforms. His manga Kōkaku Kidōtai—published internationally as The Ghost in the Shell—began in 1989. Thirty-seven years later, its official global site announced that another animation is in production.

The October 23 notice is deliberately brief. Science SARU, the studio behind the 2026 television anime Ghost in the Shell: The Ghost in the Shell, will produce the new work. The official announcement does not yet supply a format, release date, episode count or staff list. Those omissions matter: “production started” is not the same as “premieres soon.”

The larger surprise is that the franchise has never depended on one definitive screen body. Its “ghost”—questions about consciousness, memory and personhood—has survived precisely because each adaptation builds a different shell around it.

One manga, several continuities

Masamune’s original work combined dense technical notes, political intrigue, comedy and philosophical speculation. Major Motoko Kusanagi leads Public Security Section 9 in a society where cyberbrains and prosthetic bodies make the boundary between human and machine unstable.

Mamoru Oshii’s 1995 theatrical film stripped the material into a cooler, more meditative form. Its city, assembled from Hong Kong-inspired density and reflections, became as memorable as its action. Kenji Kawai’s choral score and the film’s slow attention to bodies and networks helped it travel far beyond anime fandom.

Actual official trailer from the Ghost in the Shell Official Channel. ©1995 Shirow Masamune/Kodansha, Bandai Visual and Manga Entertainment.

Stand Alone Complex, beginning in 2002 under director Kenji Kamiyama, created another continuity with longer investigations and a different balance between procedural storytelling and political theory. Arise later reconfigured origins. SAC_2045 used full 3D computer animation. The 2017 live-action film introduced the property to another audience while provoking debate over adaptation and casting.

Why Science SARU changes the texture

Science SARU is important not because one studio guarantees one look, but because it has built a reputation for elastic movement and graphic experimentation. The company’s projects have included Keep Your Hands Off Eizouken!, Inu-Oh, Scott Pilgrim Takes Off and Dandadan. Their surfaces differ dramatically.

The 2026 television series already returned the franchise to a 2D visual language closer to the manga’s expressive energy than the solemn image many overseas viewers associate with the 1995 movie. Yesterday’s announcement says the studio will continue, but it does not say the new production will repeat that series’ exact approach.

That uncertainty is productive. Ghost in the Shell is about systems that copy, alter and authenticate information. Every adaptation forces viewers to decide which traits make the work itself: Kusanagi, Section 9, cyberbrains, political conspiracies, or the philosophical problem named in the title.

A product launch and a production announcement

Today also brings a smaller physical “shell.” GEEKS RULE is releasing a limited long-sleeve shirt using imagery from the 2026 television anime at Dover Street Market Ginza’s open house. The official site announced the collaboration on October 16. It is merchandise, not the new animation, but the timing shows how contemporary anime circulates simultaneously as broadcast work, design object and global fashion signal.

That commercial reach does not explain the franchise’s endurance by itself. Plenty of properties produce merchandise. Ghost in the Shell remains unusually reusable because the questions age faster than the hardware. If memory can be edited, what counts as testimony? If a mind is distributed across networks, where does legal responsibility sit? If the body is replaceable, what remains continuous?

In 1989 those questions looked like cyberpunk. In 2026, biometric identity, synthetic media, autonomous systems and platform surveillance make them feel less like distant scenery. The predictions were never a checklist of gadgets. They were pressure tests for the institutions around technology.

What to watch next

The responsible reading of yesterday’s news is narrow: a new animation is in production at Science SARU. There is no confirmed date or format in the announcement. Fans should watch the official global site for the title, principal staff, distribution and first footage rather than treat speculation as fact.

The Japanese title contains today’s useful word: kōkaku, 攻殻. It is a coined compound often rendered “armored shell”: 攻 suggests attack, and 殻 means shell or husk. It is not ordinary daily vocabulary; readers will mainly encounter it in this title. The official English name chooses the philosophical “ghost” and “shell” instead of translating the full Japanese phrase literally.

A new production therefore arrives with an old challenge. It must look like the future without becoming trapped in an earlier decade’s image of it. This franchise has solved that problem before by letting its ghost move.
